description: Hey! We are team The 4th Dimension. Let's learn about abandoned Nasa equipment and keep them alive.
summary: Robo Pet Station is a browser game where children ages 7-12 adopt a robo pet inspired by real NASA machines left behind in space, such as the Apollo Lunar Rover, Spirit and much more. Kids learn the machine’s true mission story, then give it a voice by writing or drawing a postcard from the robot’s point of view, using real facts. Each postcard becomes a collectible trading card and an exhibit on a shared Class Museum Wall.
details:
There’s a rover on Mars called Spirit. NASA built it to last 90 days, and it kept going for more than six years, until it got stuck in soft sand and went silent in 2010. Most kids have never heard that story, so we built a game to tell it.

What it does. In Robo Pet Station, a student joins with a nickname and a class code, then picks a real NASA machine (the Apollo Lunar Rover, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity or Voyager 1) and builds a robo pet inspired by it. Each pet comes with a kid-friendly mission file: where the machine is, what it discovered and why it went quiet. Then the student writes or draws a postcard from the robot’s point of view, using real facts. The postcard becomes a printable trading card and an exhibit on the Class Museum Wall, where classmates react with stickers.

Why it matters. Kids learn real science by caring about a character instead of memorizing facts, and teachers get a safe, ready-made storytelling lesson. We hope children remember these machines and keep NASA’s abandoned hardware from being forgotten.

What we used. A browser-based web application built with React, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, using Vite as the development and build tool and hosted on GitHub Pages. AI tools, including ChatGPT, assisted with coding and development. NASA data and resources were used to provide educational content about the Moon, Mars, Voyager, and NASA missions, including NASA’s Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon and other NASA mission resources.

What makes it creative. Instead of a quiz, kids adopt a machine and speak for it. That one idea turns facts into feelings.

What we considered. Child safety (nicknames only, no chat, sticker-only reactions), accuracy (postcards must use real mission facts), and classroom reality (works on phones and cheap devices, with read-aloud support).

Next. Voice postcards, a teacher view, more machines, and Bangla and other languages.
